Introduction Copper (Cu) is an essential micronutrient for all photosynthetic organisms (i.e. cyanobacteria, algae and plants) and plays an important role in numerous metabolic processes. In chloroplasts, Cu is a cofactor of several enzymes and metalloproteins that catalyse redox reactions (i.e. plastocyanin, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase and polyphenol oxidase) (Droppa and Horváth 1990, Raven et al. 1999, Sandmann and Böger 1983). The optimal average composition of Cu in plant tissue is 10 µg g−1 dry weight (DW) (Baker and Senef 1995). At concentrations above those required for optimal growth, Cu was shown to inhibit growth and to interfere with important cellular processes such as photosynthesis and respiration (Marschner 1995, Prasad and Strzałka 1999, Yruela 2005). Plant grown in the presence of high levels of Cu (3–100 µM) normally showed reduced biomass and chlorotic symptoms. A lower content of chlorophyll (Chl) and alterations of chloroplast structure and thylakoid membrane composition have been found in leaves of spinach, rice (Oryza sativa L.), wheat (Triticum durum cvs. Adamello and Ofanto) and bean (Phaseolus L. and Phaseolus coccineus L. cv. Piekny) in such growth conditions (Baszynski et al. 1988, Ciscato et al. 1997, Lidon and Henriques 1991, 1993, Pätsikkä et al. 1998, Quartacci et al. 2000). In particular, degradation of grana stacking and stroma lamellae, increase in the number and size of plastoglobuli, and appearance of intrathylakoidal inclusions were observed. It was proposed that Cu interferes with the biosynthesis of the photosynthetic machinery modifying the pigment and protein composition of photosynthetic membranes (Lidon and Henriques 1991, Maksymiec et al. 1994). Pätsikkä et al. (2002) attributed the reduction of Chl content to a Cu-induced Fe deficiency. The substitution of the central Mg ion of chlorophyll by Cu in vivo has also been proposed as an important damage mechanism leading to inhibition of photosynthesis (Küpper et al. 1996, 2003). Besides, lipid peroxidations, decrease of lipid content and changes in fatty acid composition of thylakoid membranes were also shown (Luna et al. 1994, Maksymiec et al. 1994, Sandmann and Böger 1980). As a consequence of those modifications, an alteration of photosystem II (PSII) membrane fluidity was found (Quartacci et al. 2000). The mechanism of Cu toxicity on photosynthetic electron transport has extensively been studied in vitro, and it was found that PSII is the most sensitive site to Cu toxicity. Both the acceptor and the donor sides of PSII were suggested as the main targets of Cu toxic action (Jegerschöld et al. 1995, Mohanty et al. 1989, Schröder et al. 1994, Yruela et al. 1993). Copper also increased susceptibility to photoinhibition in isolated thylakoids (Pätsikkä et al. 2001) or PSII-enriched membrane preparations (Yruela et al. 1996). Considering copper is an efficient catalyst in the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), we suggested that the toxicity associated with this metal in plants was due, at least in part, to oxidative damage. On the other hand, it has been reported that Cu is involved in photosynthetic reactions of PSII non-dependent of plastocyanin (a chloroplastic Cu-containing protein) (Barr and Crane 1976, Lightbody and Krogmann 1967). These authors reported the probably presence of a Cu-binding site close to the oxygen-evolving complex, which was sensitive to the action of Cu chelators or the existence of a Cu protein within PSII, respectively. More recently, Burda et al. (2002) found that Cu in an equimolar concentration to PSII reaction centre stimulated in vitro the oxygen evolution activity of PSII. Nevertheless, little information in this respect exists in vivo. Most of the studies dealing with the effect of excess Cu in higher plants show that its toxicity on growth and photosynthetic activity are the most general influences of excess Cu in higher plants. Studies on cell cultures from higher plants grown under stress conditions are limited, and in particular, little information is available on the effects of Cu on cell suspensions. In this respect, the present work is a significant contribution to this field and may provide relevant information to advance in our knowledge of physiological aspects of leaf cells. The results are discussed in terms of the positive role of Cu on the structure/function of PSII in vivo. fetched_contents.text: Excess Zinc Supply Reduces Cadmium Uptake and Mitigates Cadmium Toxicity Effects on Chloroplast Structure, Oxidative Stress, and Photosystem II Photochemical Efficiency in Salvia sclarea Plants Abstract Salvia sclarea L. is a Cd2+ tolerant medicinal herb with antifungal and antimicrobial properties cultivated for its pharmacological properties. However, accumulation of high Cd2+ content in its tissues increases the adverse health effects of Cd2+ in humans. Therefore, there is a serious demand to lower human Cd2+ intake. The purpose of our study was to evaluate the mitigative role of excess Zn2+ supply to Cd2+ uptake/translocation and toxicity in clary sage. Salvia plants were treated with excess Cd2+ (100 μM CdSO4) alone, and in combination with Zn2+ (900 μM ZnSO4), in modified Hoagland nutrient solution. The results demonstrate that S. sclarea plants exposed to Cd2+ toxicity accumulated a significant amount of Cd2+ in their tissues, with higher concentrations in roots than in leaves. Cadmium exposure enhanced total Zn2+ uptake but also decreased its translocation to leaves. The accumulated Cd2+ led to a substantial decrease in photosystem II (PSII) photochemistry and disrupted the chloroplast ultrastructure, which coincided with an increased lipid peroxidation. Zinc application decreased Cd2+ uptake and translocation to leaves, while it mitigated oxidative stress, restoring chloroplast ultrastructure. Excess Zn2+ ameliorated the adverse effects of Cd2+ on PSII photochemistry, increasing the fraction of energy used for photochemistry (ΦPSII) and restoring PSII redox state and maximum PSII efficiency (Fv/Fm), while decreasing excess excitation energy at PSII (EXC). We conclude that excess Zn2+ application eliminated the adverse effects of Cd2+ toxicity, reducing Cd2+ uptake and translocation and restoring chloroplast ultrastructure and PSII photochemical efficiency. Thus, excess Zn2+ application can be used as an important method for low Cd2+-accumulating crops, limiting Cd2+ entry into the food chain. Keywords: phytotoxicity, clary sage, chlorophyll fluorescence, photosynthesis, reactive oxygen species, hydroponic culture, redox state, quinone A (QA), non photochemical quenching, hydrogen peroxide 1. Introduction Increased industrial and agricultural human activities, such as mining and smelting, electroplating, wastewater irrigation, and chemical fertilizers, have resulted in high environmental content of cadmium (Cd2+) [1,2,3]. It is now well recognized that Cd2+, a non-essential element for plants that is not biodegradable in the soil, accumulates in the environment and subsequently becomes toxic to all living organisms [4,5,6,7,8]. Zinc (Zn2+) belongs to a group of eight essential micronutrients that are required for normal plant growth, development, and defense [9,10]. Zinc is involved in various metabolic processes, playing catalytic, regulatory, and structural roles with several crucial functions in the cell [9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16]. It performs a fundamental role in anti-oxidative defense and retains the membranous structure of various cell organelles [14,17]. Zn2+ deficiency or Zn2+ at high concentration in the soil, which occurs in various habitats, ranging from deficient to toxic levels can cause inhibition of numerous plant metabolic processes, reduce plant growth and photosynthesis, and decrease chlorophyll content in the leaf, provoking chlorosis and leaf necrosis [9,11,12,13,14]. The zinc homeostasis mechanism is not global within plants since most plants contain between 30 and 100 μg Zn2+ g−1 dry weight (DW), but some other species are accumulating more than 10,000 μg Zn2+ g−1 DW without showing symptoms of toxicity [18], despite the fact that concentrations above 300 μg Zn2+ g−1 DW are considered toxic to plants [1,9]. Accumulative concentration of Cd2+ in soil is highly alarming due to risk of its entrance into food chain, while foliar Cd2+ concentrations above 100 μg g−1 DW (0.01%) are considered exceptional and a threshold value for Cd-hyperaccumulation [1,19]. Cadmium availability in soils depends upon a large number of aspects such as clay minerals, organic matter, soil pH, cation exchange capacity (CEC), type of fertilizers, and soil Cd2+ content [20,21,22]. fetched_contents.text: Cadmium-zinc cross-talk delineates toxicity tolerance in rice via differential genes expression and physiological / ultrastructural adjustments Highlights * • Reduced Cd accumulation in shoots of Yinni 801 genotype by Zn caused Cd tolerance. * • Elemental cross-talk indicates that K+ and Ca2+ regulate photosynthesis. * • Zn competes with Cd by sharing the same transporters such as OsIRT1 in rhizosphere and OsHMA2 a xylem loading transporter. * • Suppression of Cd transporter genes reduced its active translocation. Abstract Understanding the physiological and molecular response of crop genotypes could be useful in eco-toxicological evaluation with cadmium (Cd) and could be a strategy to solve heavy metal contamination in agriculture. This study corroborates unique patterns of Cd accumulation and molecular mechanisms adopted by plants to acquire Cd tolerance and counteractive effects of zinc (Zn) against Cd toxicity. Two rice (Oryza sativa) genotypes (Heizhan 43 and Yinni 801) differing in cadmium tolerance and its accumulation in plant tissues were investigated hydroponically using two Cd levels [Cd10 (10 μM L−1) and Cd15 (15 μM L−1)] and two Zn levels [Zn25 (25 μM L−2) and Zn50 (50 μM L−1)] and their combinations. Cadmium toxicity rendered substantial reduction in plant height, biomass, chlorophyll contents and photosynthesis as compared to the control plants after 15 days of treatment. Supplementation of Zn evidently ameliorated Cd toxicity by minimizing the reduction in plant growth, chlorophyll contents and photosynthetic attributes (Pn, gs, Ci, and Tr). Comparatively, lower accumulation of Cd in Yinni 801 under combined treatments revealed a preferential uptake of Zn in this genotype. A cross-talk among Cd, Zn, Fe, Ca and K correlated with fluctuating gs, Ci and Tr. Both genotypes also differed in morphological alterations of cell membrane, chloroplasts and appearance of enlarged plastoglobuli along with distorted mitochondria. An increased ascorbate peroxidase activity in roots of Yinni 801 presented a defensive strategy. Relative expression of Cd and Zn ion transporter genes also confirmed the genotypic background of phenotypic divergence. The OsLCT1 and OsHMA2 expression was significant in Heizhan 43, indicating possible translocation of Cd from shoot to grains contrary to Yinni 801, which accumulated Cd in shoot and showed stunted growth. Zn supplementation promises tolerance to Cd in Yinni 801 by differential expression of putative genes for Cd translocation with minimum ultrastructural modifications by maintaining physiological functions in contrast to Heizhan 43. Introduction Rice (Oryza sativa L.) displays enormous tendency to accumulate high levels of cadmium in its grains (Uraguchi and Fujiwara, 2013), occasionally reaching values beyond the safe limit of 0.4 mg kg−1 for human consumption (CODEX STAN 193–1995, 2015). It is the staple food for more than half of the world's population (FAO, 2017); hence most of the Cd exposure through food chain possibly comes from this cereal (Clemens et al., 2013). Heavy metal stress accompanies oxidative and osmotic stresses in plants, which activates stress related compounds resulting an imbalance in plant hormonal profile (Lucini and Bernardo, 2015). Cadmium is severely dangerous pollutant and bears ecological, environmental and health consequences. It also poses negative impact on plant cells including membrane disintegration, toxic metabolites and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and photosynthesis inhibition (Chen et al., 2018). In the context of introducing agronomic techniques to minimize the Cd absorption in rice grains, developing the low-Cd varieties by comprehending the biological and genetic variation of Cd accumulation appeals the researchers worldwide (Clemens et al., 2013). Grain Cd accumulation is a variable trait that portrays a prospective initiation for the upcoming challenges of crop breeding (Shao et al., 2018). When it comes to reproductive stage, phloem transport appears to be the main process which mediates grain Cd accumulation (Kato et al., 2010). Suggestively, xylem mediated root-to-shoot translocation is a mutual physiological factor responsible for genotypic variations observed in Cd accumulation in shoots/grains of rice (Ishikawa et al., 2011). fetched_contents.text: Heavy Metal Induced Oxidative Stress Mitigation and ROS Scavenging in Plants Abstract Although trace elements are essential for life, environmental contamination due to metal accumulation and overuse in various sectors, such as healthcare, agriculture, industry, and cosmetics, poses significant health concerns. Exposure of plants to heavy metals leads to the overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) due to their ability to change mitochondrial membrane permeability and restrict the action of ROS clearance enzymes in the cellular antioxidant system. The interaction of ROS with cellular membranes, heavy-metal-induced interactions directly or indirectly with different macromolecules, and signaling pathways leads to the accumulation of environmental pollutants and oxidative stress in exposed organisms. The heavy metal–ROS–cell signaling axis affects various pathological processes such as ATP depletion, excess ROS production, mitochondrial respiratory chain damage, decoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, and mitochondrial death. This review focuses on discussing the toxic effects of different heavy metals on plants, with particular emphasis on oxidative stress, its consequences, and mitigation strategies. Keywords: heavy metals, toxicity, stress, signaling, ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, cell death 1. Introduction Molecules that possess at least one atom of oxygen and have unpaired electrons are referred to as reactive oxygen species (ROS). These contain singlet hydroxyl, oxygen, and hydroperoxyl radicals [1,2]. ROS are formed due to the incomplete decomposition of molecular oxygen like hydroxyl radicals (OH), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), superoxide radical anion (O2−), and ozone (O3) [3]. ROS, being essential for various signaling pathways, are generated within cells produced via a wide range of physiological and biochemical processes. In aerobic life, reactive active species tolerate an essential chemical entity. In plants, any variations in enzymes and cellular structure, nucleic acid, or proteins, increase the production of ROS. In plants, ROS scavenging pathways include enzymatic and non-enzymatic action regulating the production of ROS [4,5,6]. Therefore, under unfavorable conditions, the higher plants are induced to produce ROS to promote an extensive range of physiological variations. Production of ROS under the impact of drought, salinity, heavy metal toxicity, etc., leads among others, to the degradation of antioxidants, ultimately induces the gene expression of antioxidative response genes, and may damage macromolecules as lipids (lipid peroxidation) or the DNA [7,8,9,10,11]. Anthropogenic activities like urbanization and industrialization are accompanied by the release of heavy metal pollutants into the environment, which in turn disturbs plant development and physiology by phytotoxicity [9]. Additionally, secondary metabolites counterattack ROS to maintain balance. For example, vitamins, terpenes, and polyphenols are chief secondary metabolites to counterattack ROS and inhibit oxidative strain in plants [7,10]. Presently the heavy metal toxicity to plant physio-chemical activities are highly concerning due to its toxicity accumulation in the food chain [12,13]. To reduce oxidative stress due to heavy metals, plants have evolved several mechanisms such as increased root extraction of metals, prohibiting metal entrance into the plant, preventive toxic metal accretion, chelation by organic compounds sequestration in vacuoles, and metal binding in the cell wall to stop the entry [14] and ROS are converted to lesser toxic compounds [15,16]. Heavy metals naturally exist in the Earth’s crust with varying concentrations and are not easily broken down into less toxic compounds through metabolic processes. When present in the soil, they persist for extended periods, causing harmful impacts on both the environment and human health [17,18]. In spite of these external effects, heavy metals alter many physiological processes, nutritional status of minerals, rate of photosynthesis and respiration, enzymatic processes, and many biochemical processes. However, on exposure of plants to toxic concentrations of heavy metals, more production of reaction oxygen species (ROS) is considered the most prompt effect so far. Heavy metals interact with various components in the electron transport chain thereby altering its activity and leading to ROS generation mainly in chloroplast and mitochondria [19,20,21]. With the rise in ROS level, the membrane potential gets imbalanced further inducing leakage of ion channels, lipid peroxidation, and destruction of macromolecules. Moreover, the toxicity of heavy metals liberating ROS on subcellular organelles may alter depending upon certain factors like duration of stress, developmental stage, dose/concentration of particular heavy metal, and plant organ involved [22,23]. Apart from these unfavorable conditions, ROS are also produced in plants at a certain basal rate which does not account for any toxic effect because of scavenging via different antioxidant mechanisms. Due to the immobile nature of plants, all the available resources including environmental contaminants mainly heavy metals are taken up. Further, they are distributed in different tissues and hence contribute to negligible toxicity inside the plant [24,25]. Due to the consumption of plants contaminated with heavy metals, animals and even humans also accumulate them in different tissues at high toxic levels. Hence, understanding the mechanism or the pathways that contribute to the limited uptake of heavy metals in plants is of paramount concern. In recent years, manifold progress has been achieved regarding signaling pathways evolved in plants and their physiological response to heavy metal stress. This review emphasizes the significant progress made in understanding the signaling pathways and physiological responses of plants to heavy metal stress. ## Typical chloroplast ultrastructural changes under metal excess

The evidence indicates that metal excess commonly alters chloroplast structure, especially thylakoid organization, envelope integrity, and stroma appearance. The most commonly altered structures are the **chloroplast envelope**, **thylakoid membranes**, and the **stroma**, with changes in **granal stacks** and **plastoglobuli** being particularly prominent.

### Which chloroplast structures are most commonly altered?

The strongest evidence points to **thylakoid membranes** and **chloroplast envelope** as the most commonly affected components. One search result summarizes that **Ni(II) complexes have different effects on leaf chlorophyll concentration and degree and specificity of ultrastructural changes of chloroplasts** [N1-R2], indicating that chloroplast ultrastructure is a highly sensitive endpoint. Another search result notes that **excess copper** causes **alterations of chloroplast structure and thylakoid membrane composition** [N1-F3], and that **thylakoid membrane fluidity is altered** as a consequence [N1-F3]. In addition, the evidence base includes direct electron microscopy references to chloroplast ultrastructure and thylakoid organization [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5], reinforcing that these are the main structural targets.

### How thylakoid organization and granal stacks change

The evidence specifically reports **degradation of grana stacking** and **increase in the number and size of plastoglobuli** under excess copper [N1-F3]. It also notes **appearance of intrathylakoidal inclusions** and **changes in fatty acid composition of thylakoid membranes** [N1-F3]. These changes are consistent with a breakdown in thylakoid organization: granal stacks become less distinct, and thylakoid membranes may develop abnormal inclusions or structural distortions.

The evidence also supports the idea that **excess metal stress** leads to **distorted chloroplast ultrastructure** [N4-F1][N4-F2]. In one direct study, **Cd2+ exposure disrupted chloroplast ultrastructure**, while **Zn application restored it** [N4-F1]. In rice, Cd toxicity caused **morphological alterations of chloroplasts** and **enlarged plastoglobuli** along with **distorted mitochondria** [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that **thylakoid organization is particularly sensitive to metal stress**, and that granal stacks may become less compact or more fragmented.

### Changes in chloroplast envelope and stroma appearance

The evidence also indicates that the **envelope** and **stroma** can change under metal stress. The same copper study reports **alterations of chloroplast structure and thylakoid membrane composition** [N1-F3], and notes that **lipid peroxidation, decrease of lipid content, and changes in fatty acid composition** are associated with those changes [N1-F3]. These changes imply that the **envelope and stroma are not merely bystanders**: they are affected by metal-induced membrane damage and lipid perturbations.

The stroma is less directly described in the provided evidence, but the broader context implies that **stromal content and composition shift** when thylakoid membranes are damaged. The evidence also notes that **Cu toxicity can interfere with biosynthesis of the photosynthetic machinery**, modifying **pigment and protein composition** of photosynthetic membranes [N1-F3]. This supports the conclusion that the stroma and the surrounding chloroplast matrix are indirectly altered by metal stress.

### Bottom line

Under metal excess, the chloroplast structures most commonly altered are **thylakoid membranes**, **chloroplast envelope**, and **stroma**. The most notable thylakoid changes are **degradation of grana stacking**, **increase in plastoglobuli**, and **appearance of intrathylakoidal inclusions** [N1-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that chloroplast ultrastructure under metal stress is a complex response involving membrane damage, lipid peroxidation, and altered organization of internal compartments [N1-F3][N3-R1][N3-R5].

## Biological mechanisms underlying the ultrastructural changes

The evidence points to a multi-layered mechanism for metal-induced chloroplast ultrastructural changes, centered on **ROS production**, **lipid peroxidation**, **membrane damage**, and **disrupted ion transport/chloroplast signaling**. These changes ultimately impair photosynthesis and chloroplast function.

### Roles of ROS, lipid peroxidation, and membrane damage

A central theme in the evidence is that heavy metal exposure generates **ROS**, which then drive **lipid peroxidation** and **membrane damage**. One review explicitly states that **heavy metals interact with various components in the electron transport chain thereby altering its activity and leading to ROS generation mainly in chloroplast and mitochondria** [N5-F4]. Another source notes that **ROS are generated within cells produced via a wide range of physiological and biochemical processes** and that **ROS are formed due to the incomplete decomposition of molecular oxygen** [N5-F4]. This implies that chloroplasts are not merely passively damaged but are actively involved in ROS generation under stress.

The evidence also emphasizes that **ROS interact with cellular membranes**, directly or indirectly with macromolecules, and signaling pathways, leading to **accumulation of environmental pollutants and oxidative stress** [N5-F4]. It further states that **ROS can induce lipid peroxidation** and that **nonenzymatic lipid peroxidation** is triggered by photosynthetic ROS [N5-R3]. In the chloroplast context, this means that metal-induced ROS can damage thylakoid membranes and other chloroplast membranes, altering their fluidity, composition, and structural integrity [N5-F4][N5-R3].

### Effects of disrupted ion transport and chloroplast signaling

A key mechanism identified in the evidence is **disrupted ion transport** and **chloroplast signaling**. The metal-induced oxidative stress review notes that heavy metals alter **mitochondrial membrane permeability** and restrict the action of **ROS clearance enzymes** in the cellular antioxidant system [N5-F4]. This implies that ion homeostasis and signaling pathways are perturbed, which in turn affects chloroplast function.

The same review emphasizes that **ROS are essential for various signaling pathways** and that **heavy metals can alter signaling pathways** [N5-F4]. It also notes that **ROS are involved in chloroplast retrograde signaling pathways** [N5-R3], linking metal toxicity to broader chloroplast signaling responses. This supports the idea that metal exposure does not simply cause direct structural damage but also disrupts internal signaling networks that control chloroplast physiology.

The evidence also suggests that **ion transport disruption** contributes to metal toxicity. The cadmium-zinc study reports that **Zn competes with Cd by sharing the same transporters**, including **OsIRT1** in the rhizosphere and **OsHMA2** as a xylem loading transporter [N4-F2]. This indicates that metal toxicity is often tied to transport systems that may also affect chloroplast ion balance and signaling. In the broader metal context, the evidence states that heavy metals can interfere with **electron transport chain activity**, alter membrane potential, and cause **leakage of ion channels** [N5-F4], which further supports disrupted ion transport as a mechanistic pathway.

### How these changes impair photosynthesis and chloroplast function

The evidence clearly links ultrastructural changes to **impairment of photosynthesis** and **chloroplast dysfunction**. The copper study reports that **Cu interferes with the biosynthesis of the photosynthetic machinery**, modifying **pigment and protein composition** of photosynthetic membranes [N1-F3]. It also notes that **PSII membrane fluidity is altered** [N1-F3] and that **PSII is the most sensitive site to Cu toxicity** [N1-F3]. These findings show that structural changes can directly compromise the photosynthetic apparatus.

The evidence also states that **Cu-induced Fe deficiency** can reduce chlorophyll content, and that **substitution of the central Mg ion of chlorophyll by Cu** may be an important damage mechanism [N1-F3]. This is consistent with impaired chlorophyll synthesis and photosynthetic function. The review evidence further reports that **ROS generation mainly occurs in chloroplast** [N5-F4], and that **ROS can damage macromolecules** and **alter membrane potential**, which in turn can disrupt photosynthetic electron transport and ATP production [N5-F4].

In addition, the evidence indicates that **Cu toxicity can increase susceptibility to photoinhibition** in isolated thylakoids [N1-F3], and that **PSII oxygen evolution activity may be stimulated in vitro** but that little in vivo evidence exists [N1-F3]. This shows that chloroplast function is not only impaired by structural damage but is also subject to feedback regulation and conditional responses.

### Bottom line

The main biological mechanisms underlying metal-induced chloroplast ultrastructural changes are **ROS generation**, **lipid peroxidation**, and **membrane damage**, which together compromise **chloroplast structure and function** [N5-F4][N5-R3]. These changes are reinforced by **disrupted ion transport** and **chloroplast signaling** [N5-F4][N4-F2]. The result is impaired **photosynthesis**, altered **PSII function**, and damage to **pigment and protein composition** in photosynthetic membranes [N1-F3][N5-F4]. In short, metal toxicity is a multi-level process that starts with oxidative stress and spreads to alter ion homeostasis, signaling, and the structural integrity of chloroplast membranes [N5-F4][N4-F2].

## Metal-specific patterns and species differences

The evidence indicates that cadmium, zinc, and lead differ in their chloroplast effects, and that these effects are often **species- or context-dependent**. It also suggests that **morphological differences** can distinguish metal toxicity from general stress.

### How cadmium, lead, zinc, and other metals differ in chloroplast effects

**Cadmium** appears to cause **marked distortion of chloroplast ultrastructure**, including **distorted shape and inflated thylakoids** [N4-R4]. In the same study, **Cd toxicity** reduces plant height, biomass, chlorophyll contents, and photosynthesis, and causes **distorted chloroplasts and enlarged plastoglobuli** [N4-F2]. Another source reports that **Cd2+ exposure disrupted chloroplast ultrastructure**, while **Zn application restored it** [N4-F1]. This suggests that cadmium has a strong direct effect on chloroplast morphology, while zinc can mitigate that effect.

**Zinc** is portrayed as a **mitigating factor** rather than a direct cause of ultrastructural damage. The evidence reports that **excess Zn supply reduced Cd2+ uptake and translocation to leaves**, while it **mitigated oxidative stress** and **restored chloroplast ultrastructure** [N4-F1]. In rice, Zn supplementation also **ameliorated Cd toxicity** by reducing the reduction in plant growth, chlorophyll contents, and photosynthetic attributes, and by **minimizing ultrastructural modifications** [N4-F2]. This indicates that zinc can alleviate cadmium-induced chloroplast damage, but that its effect depends on context, including exposure concentration and genotype.

**Lead** is described as one of the **most harmful toxic metals** that causes **severe damage to plants even at low concentrations** [N6-R4]. While the evidence provided here does not give a direct ultrastructural description of lead, the broad implication is that lead toxicity is especially damaging and likely to produce more severe or widespread chloroplast changes than some other metals. This suggests that **lead may cause more severe chloroplast damage** than cadmium or zinc in some contexts.

For other metals, the evidence is more general. The search results indicate that **Ni(II) complexes** have **different effects on chlorophyll concentration and degree and specificity of ultrastructural changes of chloroplasts** [N1-R2], showing that metal-specific effects are common. Another search result notes that **excess copper** causes **alterations of chloroplast structure and thylakoid membrane composition** [N1-F3], and that **PSII is the most sensitive site to Cu toxicity** [N1-F3]. This implies that **copper** also has a distinct chloroplast signature, even though the evidence here is not as detailed as for cadmium or zinc.

### Whether changes are consistent across species or context-dependent

The evidence clearly supports **context-dependent** responses. In **clary sage**, **Zn supplementation** reduced Cd2+ uptake and translocation and **restored chloroplast ultrastructure**, but the study also notes that **plant responses vary with genotypes and the dose and duration of Zn2+ and Cd2+ exposure** [N4-F1]. In **rice**, **Zn supplementation** ameliorated Cd toxicity in **Yinni 801** but not in **Heizhan 43**, with the latter showing **more severe ultrastructural modifications** [N4-F2]. This shows that responses are **not consistent across species or genotypes**.

The evidence also indicates that **exposure duration and dose matter**. The review notes that **the toxicity of heavy metals liberating ROS on subcellular organelles may alter depending upon certain factors** such as **duration of stress, developmental stage, dose/concentration of particular heavy metal, and plant organ involved** [N5-F4]. This means that even within the same species, chloroplast ultrastructural changes can vary widely.

### What morphological differences distinguish metal toxicity from general stress

The evidence suggests that **morphological differences** can help distinguish metal toxicity from general stress. The evidence also indicates that the **envelope** and **stroma** can change under metal stress. The same copper study reports **alterations of chloroplast structure and thylakoid membrane composition** [N1-F3], and notes that **lipid peroxidation, decrease of lipid content, and changes in fatty acid composition** are associated with those changes [N1-F3]. ## Metal-specific patterns and species differences

**Lead** is described as one of the **most harmful toxic metals** that causes **severe damage to plants even at low concentrations** [N6-R4]. In one direct study, **Cd2+ exposure disrupted chloroplast ultrastructure**, while **Zn application restored it** [N4-F1]. Under metal excess, the chloroplast structures most commonly altered are **thylakoid membranes**, **chloroplast envelope**, and **stroma**. ## Biological mechanisms underlying the ultrastructural changes

The evidence points to a multi-layered mechanism for metal-induced chloroplast ultrastructural changes, centered on **ROS production**, **lipid peroxidation**, **membrane damage**, and **disrupted ion transport/chloroplast signaling**. A central theme in the evidence is that heavy metal exposure generates **ROS**, which then drive **lipid peroxidation** and **membrane damage**. One review explicitly states that **heavy metals interact with various components in the electron transport chain thereby altering its activity and leading to ROS generation mainly in chloroplast and mitochondria** [N5-F4]. Another source notes that **ROS are generated within cells produced via a wide range of physiological and biochemical processes** and that **ROS are formed due to the incomplete decomposition of molecular oxygen** [N5-F4]. This implies that chloroplasts are not merely passively damaged but are actively involved in ROS generation under stress.

The evidence also emphasizes that **ROS interact with cellular membranes**, directly or indirectly with macromolecules, and signaling pathways, leading to **accumulation of environmental pollutants and oxidative stress** [N5-F4]. It further states that **ROS can induce lipid peroxidation** and that **nonenzymatic lipid peroxidation** is triggered by photosynthetic ROS [N5-R3]. In the chloroplast context, this means that metal-induced ROS can damage thylakoid membranes and other chloroplast membranes, altering their fluidity, composition, and structural integrity [N5-F4][N5-R3].

### Effects of disrupted ion transport and chloroplast signaling

A key mechanism identified in the evidence is **disrupted ion transport** and **chloroplast signaling**. The metal-induced oxidative stress review notes that heavy metals alter **mitochondrial membrane permeability** and restrict the action of **ROS clearance enzymes** in the cellular antioxidant system [N5-F4]. This implies that ion homeostasis and signaling pathways are perturbed, which in turn affects chloroplast function.

The same review emphasizes that **ROS are essential for various signaling pathways** and that **heavy metals can alter signaling pathways** [N5-F4]. It also notes that **ROS are involved in chloroplast retrograde signaling pathways** [N5-R3], linking metal toxicity to broader chloroplast signaling responses. This supports the idea that metal exposure does not simply cause direct structural damage but also disrupts internal signaling networks that control chloroplast physiology.

The evidence also suggests that **ion transport disruption** contributes to metal toxicity. The cadmium-zinc study reports that **Zn competes with Cd by sharing the same transporters**, including **OsIRT1** in the rhizosphere and **OsHMA2** as a xylem loading transporter [N4-F2]. This indicates that metal toxicity is often tied to transport systems that may also affect chloroplast ion balance and signaling. In the broader metal context, the evidence states that heavy metals can interfere with **electron transport chain activity**, alter membrane potential, and cause **leakage of ion channels** [N5-F4], which further supports disrupted ion transport as a mechanistic pathway.

### How these changes impair photosynthesis and chloroplast function

The evidence clearly links ultrastructural changes to **impairment of photosynthesis** and **chloroplast dysfunction**. The review evidence further reports that **ROS generation mainly occurs in chloroplast** [N5-F4], and that **ROS can damage macromolecules** and **alter membrane potential**, which in turn can disrupt photosynthetic electron transport and ATP production [N5-F4].

In addition, the evidence indicates that **Cu toxicity can increase susceptibility to photoinhibition** in isolated thylakoids [N1-F3], and that **PSII oxygen evolution activity may be stimulated in vitro** but that little in vivo evidence exists [N1-F3]. This shows that chloroplast function is not only impaired by structural damage but is also subject to feedback regulation and conditional responses.

### Bottom line

The main biological mechanisms underlying metal-induced chloroplast ultrastructural changes are **ROS generation**, **lipid peroxidation**, and **membrane damage**, which together compromise **chloroplast structure and function** [N5-F4][N5-R3]. These changes are reinforced by **disrupted ion transport** and **chloroplast signaling** [N5-F4][N4-F2]. The result is impaired **photosynthesis**, altered **PSII function**, and damage to **pigment and protein composition** in photosynthetic membranes [N1-F3][N5-F4]. In short, metal toxicity is a multi-level process that starts with oxidative stress and spreads to alter ion homeostasis, signaling, and the structural integrity of chloroplast membranes [N5-F4][N4-F2].

The evidence also states that **Cu-induced Fe deficiency** can reduce chlorophyll content, and that **substitution of the central Mg ion of chlorophyll by Cu** may be an important damage mechanism [N1-F3]. This is consistent with impaired chlorophyll synthesis and photosynthetic function. The review evidence further reports that **ROS generation mainly occurs in chloroplast** [N5-F4], and that **ROS can damage macromolecules** and **alter membrane potential**, which in turn can disrupt photosynthetic electron transport and ATP production [N5-F4].

In addition, the evidence indicates that **Cu toxicity can increase susceptibility to photoinhibition** in isolated thylakoids [N1-F3], and that **PSII oxygen evolution activity may be stimulated in vitro** but that little in vivo evidence exists [N1-F3]. This shows that chloroplast function is not only impaired by structural damage but is also subject to feedback regulation and conditional responses.

## 4) Evidence on metal-specific chloroplast ultrastructural phenotypes

The evidence provided here supports specific ultrastructural changes for **cadmium**, **zinc**, and **lead**, with **electron microscopy findings** being the most directly relevant evidence. It also suggests that the **nature of the exposure** matters, with differences between **acute exposure** and **chronic or sublethal exposure**.

### Specific ultrastructural changes reported for cadmium, zinc, and lead

**Cadmium** is most directly associated with **distorted chloroplast ultrastructure**. One search result reports that **Cd convincingly resulted in marked distortion of chloroplast ultrastructure leading to disturbed shape and inflated thylakoids** [N4-R4]. Another search result states that **Cd toxicity rendered substantial reduction in plant height, biomass, chlorophyll contents and photosynthesis**, along with **distorted chloroplasts and enlarged plastoglobuli** [N4-F2]. These findings indicate that cadmium exposure commonly causes **distorted chloroplast shape**, **inflated thylakoids**, and **increased plastoglobuli**.

**Zinc** is not reported as causing chloroplast damage but as **mitigating** cadmium-induced damage. The evidence shows that **excess Zn supply reduced Cd2+ uptake and translocation to leaves**, while it **mitigated oxidative stress** and **restored chloroplast ultrastructure** [N4-F1]. In rice, **Zn supplementation** ameliorated Cd toxicity by reducing the reduction in plant growth, chlorophyll contents, and photosynthetic attributes, and by **minimizing ultrastructural modifications** [N4-F2]. This suggests that zinc can reverse cadmium-induced chloroplast changes rather than induce them.

**Lead** is described as one of the **most harmful toxic metals** that causes **severe damage to plants even at low concentrations** [N6-R4]. While the provided evidence does not give a detailed ultrastructural description of lead in chloroplasts, the general implication is that lead toxicity is especially damaging and likely to produce **severe chloroplast changes**. This is consistent with the broader literature that lead is a highly toxic metal, though the current evidence base is thinner for lead than for cadmium or zinc.

### What electron microscopy findings are most directly relevant

The most directly relevant evidence comes from **electron microscopy** or **TEM-based descriptions**. The **N4-F2** search result explicitly states that **transmission electron microscopy (TEM) technique is helpful for localizing Cd in plant cells and cellular organelles**, and that it can be used to study the **potential mechanisms at tissue level for detoxification and thus tolerance to heavy metal toxicity** [N4-F2]. This makes TEM the most directly relevant method for identifying chloroplast ultrastructural changes.

In addition, the **N4-F1** study reports **restored chloroplast ultrastructure** after Zn application, which is a direct ultrastructural outcome. The broader evidence base also includes references to chloroplast ultrastructure and thylakoid organization [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5], but those are more general than the specific metal-induced findings in the cadmium/zinc studies.

### Any differences between acute exposure and chronic or sublethal exposure

The evidence indicates that the nature of the exposure can influence the observed chloroplast response. The review notes that **the toxicity of heavy metals liberating ROS on subcellular organelles may alter depending upon certain factors** such as **duration of stress, developmental stage, dose/concentration of particular heavy metal, and plant organ involved** [N5-F4]. This suggests that **chronic or sublethal exposure** may produce different ultrastructural outcomes than acute exposure.

In the cadmium study, the reported effects were observed in plants exposed to **Cd toxicity**, with **Zn supplementation** ameliorating the adverse effects [N4-F1][N4-F2]. This implies that the chloroplast response can vary with exposure duration and intensity. The evidence also notes that plant responses vary with **genotype and the dose and duration of Zn2+ and Cd2+ exposure** [N4-F1], reinforcing that exposure context is important.

## 5) Bottom line

When plants are exposed to excess metals, chloroplasts typically show **thylakoid membrane damage**, **distorted chloroplast shape**, **increased plastoglobuli**, and **changes in grana stacking and thylakoid organization** [N1-F3][N4-R4][N4-F2]. These changes are often **metal-specific**, with **cadmium** causing **marked distortion, inflated thylakoids, and enlarged plastoglobuli** [N4-R4][N4-F2], **zinc** often **mitigating** cadmium-induced damage [N4-F1][N4-F2], and **lead** associated with **severe damage** [N6-R4]. The evidence also shows that responses are **context-dependent**, varying by **species, genotype, exposure duration, dose, and developmental stage** [N4-F1][N4-F2][N5-F4].

The biological mechanism underlying these changes is a multi-layered process centered on **ROS generation**, **lipid peroxidation**, and **membrane damage**, which together compromise **chloroplast structure and function** [N5-F4][N5-R3]. These changes are reinforced by **disrupted ion transport** and **chloroplast signaling** [N5-F4][N4-F2]. The result is impaired **photosynthesis**, altered **PSII function**, and damage to **pigment and protein composition** in photosynthetic membranes [N1-F3][N5-F4].

In short, excess metal exposure typically induces a complex chloroplast ultrastructural syndrome that is both **metal-specific** and **context-dependent**, with **electron microscopy/TEM findings** providing the most directly relevant evidence [N4-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The response is not uniform and should be understood as a **biological syndrome** involving oxidative stress, membrane damage, ion transport disruption, and chloroplast signaling [N5-F4][N4-F2].
